ety.text: 19th century: from German Chromosom, ultimately from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “colour”) + σῶμα (sôma, “body”) (because they are stained under the microscope). Equivalent to chromo- + -some.

senses.d: A linear arrangement of condensed DNA and associated proteins (such as chaperone proteins) which contains the genetic material (genome) of an organism.
ex: A length of DNA is divided into segments called chromosomes and shorter individual units called genes.

ety.text: From chronical, from Old French cronike, from Latin chronicus, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). By surface analysis, chron- + -ic.

senses.d: Being problematic over an extended period of time.
ex: chronic unemployment; chronic poverty; chronic anger; chronic life
chronic cough; chronic headache; chronic illness
So dreadful was the concentration of his glare that it seemed as if it must become chronic and stay like that for ever.

senses.d: Of a person, suffering from an affliction that is prolonged or slow to heal.
ex: Chronic patients must learn to live with their condition.
They left him in a chronic condition.
That was cool, chronic in fact.
It's ironic, I had the brew, she had the chronic

senses.d: A condition of extended duration, either continuous or marked by frequent recurrence. Sometimes implies a condition which worsens with each recurrence, though that is not inherent in the term.
A person who is chronic, such as a criminal reoffender or a person with chronic disease.
ex: Of fifty-five boys scoring four or more, fifteen were chronic offenders (out of twenty-three chronics altogether) […]
